title: Cardiovascular Foundations
subject: Physiology
description: Build a working model of the heart: trace circulation, connect electrical and mechanical events, and distinguish the determinants of cardiac output through short lessons and original practice questions.
review_note: Original pilot material. Editorial review pending.

rights.content: Original Athena pilot lessons and questions; external sources linked for reference.

concepts.title: Blood flow through the heart
concepts.objective: Trace a complete adult circulation loop and classify a vessel by its direction of flow.
concepts.lesson: Think of circulation as two connected loops. Blood returning from the body enters the right atrium, crosses into the right ventricle, and travels through the pulmonary arteries to the lungs. It returns through pulmonary veins to the left atrium, enters the left ventricle, and leaves through the aorta for the body. An artery carries blood away from the heart; a vein carries it toward the heart. Oxygen content is a separate property. To check a route, name the chamber, destination, and vessel direction at each step. In steady circulation, both ventricles move equal volumes over time, although they generate different pressures.
key_points: Right ventricle → pulmonary arteries → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium.
Left ventricle → aorta → body → systemic veins → right atrium.
Artery and vein describe flow direction, not oxygen content.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e: Heart Anatomy
sources.section: 19.1 — Chambers and Circulation through the Heart

questions.prompt: In normal adult circulation, blood leaving the right ventricle next enters which vessel?
questions.explanation: The right ventricle supplies the pulmonary circuit through the pulmonary trunk, which divides into pulmonary arteries. Follow the destination to choose the route: this blood is heading to the lungs. The aorta receives left ventricular output, while pulmonary veins and the venae cavae carry blood back toward the heart.
misconceptions: Confuses the right ventricular outlet with the left ventricular outlet.
Reverses the direction of flow in pulmonary veins.
Confuses venous return to the right atrium with output from the right ventricle.

questions.prompt: A diagram labels a vessel carrying relatively oxygen-poor blood away from the heart toward the lungs. How should it be classified?
options: A systemic vein, because its oxygen content is low
A pulmonary vein, because it connects to the lungs
A systemic artery, because it leaves the heart
A pulmonary artery, because it leaves the heart for the lungs
questions.explanation: Classify the direction first: a vessel taking blood away from the heart is an artery. Its destination identifies the pulmonary circuit. Oxygen-poor blood does not make a vessel a vein. Pulmonary arteries provide the clearest reminder that flow direction and oxygen content answer different questions.
misconceptions: Uses oxygen content instead of direction to define a vein.
Uses the lung destination without checking the direction of flow.
Recognizes arterial direction but assigns the wrong circulation circuit.

questions.prompt: In a steady-state model with no shunts, the left ventricle pumps 5 L/min. What average flow must the right ventricle pump?
options: A larger flow because its wall is thinner
questions.explanation: The two circuits are connected in series, so their average flows must match in this steady-state model. The right ventricle therefore pumps 5 L/min. Unequal sustained flows would accumulate blood in one circuit. Differences in ventricular wall thickness and pressure do not require different average pumped volumes.
misconceptions: Divides a serial circulation's flow between the two ventricles as if they were parallel branches.
Adds the same circulating flow twice.
Confuses the pressure generated by a ventricle with the volume it must deliver.

concepts.title: Valves and pressure gradients
concepts.objective: Identify the four valves and predict opening or closure from upstream and downstream pressures.
concepts.lesson: A heart valve is a gate controlled by the pressure difference across it. The tricuspid valve joins the right atrium to the right ventricle; the mitral valve joins the left atrium to the left ventricle. The pulmonary and aortic valves sit at the ventricular exits. Forward pressure opens a normal valve, while a reversed gradient closes it. Papillary muscles and chordae tendineae support the atrioventricular valve leaflets during ventricular contraction; they prevent the leaflets from being displaced into the atria. When solving a valve question, sketch the two adjoining spaces and compare their pressures before deciding whether flow can occur.
key_points: Tricuspid and mitral valves guard the atrium-to-ventricle openings.
Pulmonary and aortic valves guard the ventricular outlets.
Pressure differences move valve leaflets; papillary muscles help prevent atrioventricular valve prolapse.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e: Heart Anatomy

questions.prompt: Which valve does blood cross when moving from the left atrium into the left ventricle?
questions.explanation: The mitral valve is the left atrioventricular valve. Its position makes it the gate between the left atrium and left ventricle. The tricuspid valve occupies the corresponding position on the right. The aortic and pulmonary valves are ventricular outlet valves, so neither belongs on this atrium-to-ventricle route.
misconceptions: Swaps the right and left atrioventricular valves.
Confuses entry into the left ventricle with its outlet.
Confuses a right ventricular outlet with a left atrioventricular opening.

questions.prompt: In a simplified model with a normal aortic valve, left ventricular pressure rises above aortic pressure during systole. What happens next?
options: The aortic valve opens and forward ejection can begin
The aortic valve closes and forward ejection begins
The mitral valve opens to permit aortic ejection
The pulmonary valve opens to empty the left ventricle
questions.explanation: The left ventricle is upstream of the aortic valve. Once its pressure exceeds the pressure downstream in the aorta, the forward gradient opens the normal valve and permits ejection. A closed outlet would prevent that flow. The mitral and pulmonary valves connect different spaces and cannot provide this outlet.
misconceptions: Assumes forward ventricular ejection occurs through a closed outlet valve.
Treats the left ventricular inlet as the aortic outlet.
Swaps the pulmonary and aortic ventricular outlets.

questions.prompt: During ventricular contraction, what is the main role of the papillary muscles and chordae tendineae?
options: Pull the semilunar valves open for ejection
Prevent atrioventricular leaflets from prolapsing into the atria
Pull the atrioventricular valves open for filling
Carry the electrical impulse directly into the aorta
questions.explanation: Rising ventricular pressure pushes the atrioventricular valve leaflets toward closure. Tension supplied through the chordae supports the leaflets so they do not prolapse into the atria. This is a stabilizing function during contraction. These structures neither operate the semilunar valves nor create the pressure gradient that opens the filling valves.
misconceptions: Assigns chordae and papillary muscles to the semilunar valves.
Mistakes leaflet support during systole for active opening during filling.
Confuses mechanical valve support with the electrical conduction pathway.

concepts.title: Cardiac electrical conduction
concepts.objective: Order the main conduction structures and distinguish electrical activation from mechanical contraction.
concepts.lesson: The normal electrical sequence starts in the sinoatrial node and spreads through the atria to the atrioventricular node. A brief delay there gives atrial contraction time to contribute to ventricular filling. The signal then passes through the atrioventricular bundle, its branches, and Purkinje fibers to activate the ventricles. Electrical activation initiates a mechanical response; the two events are related but are not interchangeable. On an ECG, the P wave represents atrial depolarization and the QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization. Practice by narrating the path aloud, then saying what muscular event follows each electrical event. This keeps a timing diagram from becoming a list of disconnected labels.
key_points: Normal activation begins in the sinoatrial node.
The atrioventricular node delays transmission before ventricular activation.
An ECG records electrical events; contraction follows activation.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e: Cardiac Muscle and Electrical Activity

questions.prompt: Which structure normally initiates the electrical sequence of a sinus heartbeat?
questions.explanation: The sinoatrial node normally sets the rhythm and starts activation of the atria. The atrioventricular node, bundle branches, and Purkinje fibers lie farther along the normal route. Distinguish the starting point from the structures that delay or distribute a signal after it has already begun.
misconceptions: Confuses the normal pacemaker with the structure that delays atrioventricular transmission.
Selects a ventricular distribution branch as the normal starting point.
Selects the terminal ventricular conduction network as the normal starting point.

questions.prompt: A teaching model removes the normal atrioventricular nodal delay but keeps the conduction route unchanged. Which timing benefit has been lost?
options: Time for aortic pressure to fall to zero
Time for the pulmonary veins to reverse their flow
Time for atrial contraction to contribute to filling before ventricular contraction
Time for ventricular contraction to finish before atrial activation begins
questions.explanation: The nodal delay separates atrial activation from ventricular activation. This timing allows atrial contraction to add to ventricular filling before ventricular systole starts. Removing the delay removes that interval. It does not imply reversed venous flow, zero aortic pressure, or an inversion of the normal activation sequence.
misconceptions: Assumes the conduction delay is needed to eliminate arterial pressure.
Assigns the delay a role in reversing pulmonary venous flow.
Reverses the normal order of atrial and ventricular activation.

questions.prompt: On an ECG teaching trace, what does the QRS complex directly represent?
questions.explanation: The QRS complex records ventricular depolarization, the electrical activation preceding ventricular contraction. Ejection is a later mechanical event requiring appropriate pressure and valve conditions. The P wave corresponds to atrial depolarization, while the T wave corresponds to ventricular repolarization. Keep the electrical trace separate from the accompanying mechanical sequence.
misconceptions: Treats an electrical ECG signal as a direct measurement of blood flow.
Swaps the QRS complex with the P wave.
Swaps the QRS complex with the T wave.

concepts.title: The cardiac cycle
concepts.objective: Infer ventricular filling, isovolumetric phases, or ejection from volume, pressure, and valve state.
concepts.lesson: Follow one ventricle through a beat. During filling, its atrioventricular valve is open and its outlet valve is closed. Contraction raises ventricular pressure; after the inlet closes, pressure rises briefly with both valves closed. This is isovolumetric contraction: pressure changes, but chamber volume does not. When ventricular pressure exceeds outlet pressure, ejection begins. Relaxation eventually closes the outlet, producing another interval with both valves closed before filling resumes. End-diastolic volume is the volume before ejection; end-systolic volume is what remains afterward. Their difference is stroke volume. For any phase, ask two questions: can blood enter or leave, and is the chamber pressure rising or falling?
key_points: Both valves are closed during isovolumetric contraction and relaxation.
Ejection starts when the ventricular outlet valve opens.
Stroke volume = end-diastolic volume − end-systolic volume.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e: Cardiac Cycle

questions.prompt: A normal left ventricle has rising pressure, a closed mitral valve, a closed aortic valve, and constant volume. Which phase fits?
questions.explanation: Both valves being closed explains the constant volume: there is no inlet or outlet flow. Rising pressure identifies contraction rather than relaxation. Ejection requires an open aortic valve, and filling requires an open mitral valve. Use the direction of pressure change to distinguish the two isovolumetric phases.
misconceptions: Assumes filling can occur while the ventricular inlet is closed.
Assumes ejection can occur while the ventricular outlet is closed.
Recognizes closed valves but overlooks the rising rather than falling pressure.

questions.prompt: A model ventricle contains 140 mL at end-diastole and 55 mL at end-systole. What volume was ejected in that beat?
questions.explanation: Subtract what remains after ejection from what was present beforehand: 140 − 55 = 85 mL. End-systolic volume is residual blood, so it is not itself the ejected amount. Adding the two chamber volumes counts blood remaining in the ventricle rather than calculating the change during systole.
misconceptions: Uses the residual end-systolic volume as the ejected volume.
Assumes the ventricle ejects its entire end-diastolic contents.
Adds the before-and-after volumes instead of subtracting them.

questions.prompt: During relaxation in a normal heart, left ventricular pressure falls below left atrial pressure while the aortic valve remains closed. Which event follows?
options: The aortic valve opens and ventricular ejection starts
Both valves stay closed throughout the remainder of diastole
The mitral valve opens and ventricular filling starts
The mitral valve closes and isovolumetric contraction starts
questions.explanation: The atrium now has the higher pressure across the mitral valve, creating a forward filling gradient into the ventricle. Opening of this inlet ends isovolumetric relaxation and permits ventricular volume to increase. The stated pressure change provides no reason for aortic ejection or for beginning a new contraction.
misconceptions: Uses an atrium-to-ventricle pressure gradient to predict opening of the ventricular outlet.
Extends isovolumetric relaxation past the point where the filling valve opens.
Confuses falling ventricular pressure during relaxation with the onset of contraction.

concepts.title: Cardiac output and units
concepts.objective: Calculate cardiac output or stroke volume with correct units and predict the effect of a stated change.
concepts.lesson: Cardiac output describes how much blood one ventricle delivers each minute. Multiply heart rate in beats per minute by stroke volume in milliliters per beat. The beat units cancel, leaving milliliters per minute; divide by 1,000 to express liters per minute. The equation also helps reason about change: a faster rate raises output only if stroke volume is maintained or changes favorably. When a problem fixes one factor, compare the other factor directly. Write the units before doing arithmetic, and state whether the result refers to one beat or one minute. This habit separates stroke volume, cardiac output, and the blood volume remaining inside a chamber.
key_points: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume.
mL/beat × beats/min = mL/min; 1,000 mL = 1 L.
Interpret changes using both rate and stroke volume.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e: Cardiac Physiology

questions.prompt: A model has a heart rate of 80 beats/min and a stroke volume of 65 mL/beat. What is its cardiac output?
questions.explanation: Multiply 80 beats/min by 65 mL/beat to obtain 5,200 mL/min. Dividing by 1,000 gives 5.2 L/min. The beats cancel, which confirms that this is a volume per minute. Adding 80 and 65 mixes unlike units, while the other numerical distractors misplace the liters conversion.
misconceptions: Converts milliliters to liters with an extra factor of ten.
Converts milliliters to liters with one factor of ten missing.
Adds heart rate and stroke volume instead of multiplying them.

questions.prompt: A model delivers 6 L/min at 100 beats/min. What is the stroke volume?
questions.explanation: Rearrange the equation: stroke volume equals cardiac output divided by heart rate. Convert 6 L/min to 6,000 mL/min, then divide by 100 beats/min to obtain 60 mL/beat. The minute units cancel. Keeping the original liters result would give 0.06 L/beat, not 0.06 mL/beat.
misconceptions: Labels a result in liters per beat as milliliters per beat.
Introduces an extra factor of ten when dividing cardiac output by rate.
Uses the heart rate's numerical value as a stroke volume.

questions.prompt: In two model states, heart rate stays at 80 beats/min while stroke volume falls from 70 to 55 mL/beat. How does cardiac output change?
questions.explanation: The initial output is 80 × 70 = 5,600 mL/min, or 5.6 L/min. The new output is 80 × 55 = 4,400 mL/min, or 4.4 L/min. Because rate is fixed, the lower volume per beat directly lowers volume per minute. Multiply the change by rate rather than subtracting it once.
misconceptions: Treats a constant heart rate as sufficient to maintain cardiac output.
Predicts a rise in output from a fall in stroke volume at unchanged rate.
Subtracts the 15 mL per-beat change only once from a per-minute output.

concepts.title: Preload and ventricular filling
concepts.objective: Recognize preload as initial myocardial stretch and predict an isolated filling change within physiological limits.
concepts.lesson: Preload concerns the starting stretch of ventricular muscle before contraction. End-diastolic volume is a useful indicator of that filling state, though volume and muscle stretch are not identical measurements. More venous return can increase filling and preload. Within physiological limits, greater initial stretch can increase stroke volume through the Frank-Starling mechanism when afterload and inotropic state are held constant. This is a loading effect; it does not by itself establish a change in intrinsic contractility. Use the phrase 'before the squeeze' as a timing cue. In an experiment, identify what changed during filling and what was deliberately kept constant before predicting the next beat.
key_points: Preload is initial myocardial stretch before contraction.
End-diastolic volume is an indicator of ventricular filling and preload.
Frank-Starling responses describe a filling-related change at a stated inotropic state.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e: Cardiac Physiology
Richard E. Klabunde: Effects of Preload, Afterload and Inotropy

questions.prompt: Which measurement is commonly used as an indicator of ventricular preload?
options: Heart rate at the sinoatrial node
questions.explanation: End-diastolic volume describes how full the ventricle is just before contraction, making it a useful indicator of initial muscle stretch. It is a surrogate rather than a direct sarcomere measurement. Aortic pressure concerns the ejection load, and end-systolic volume describes what remains after the beat rather than the initial filling state.
misconceptions: Uses a rate measurement as a measure of initial ventricular stretch.
Confuses the load during ejection with the filling state before contraction.
Uses post-ejection residual volume as the pre-contraction filling measure.

questions.prompt: A controlled model increases venous return and end-diastolic volume while keeping aortic pressure and inotropic state fixed. Which determinant has directly increased?
options: Afterload, because more blood must be ejected
Intrinsic contractility, because more blood enters
Preload, because initial ventricular filling increased
Heart rate, because filling volume increased
questions.explanation: The stated intervention increases the volume present before contraction, so it changes preload. The problem explicitly holds aortic pressure and inotropic state fixed. A larger filling volume may produce a stronger beat through Frank-Starling behavior without requiring a change in intrinsic contractility. No change in heart rate is specified.
misconceptions: Treats increased filling as a direct increase in the ejection load despite fixed outlet pressure.
Attributes a filling-related response to altered inotropy despite the stated control.
Infers a rate change from a volume change without supporting information.

questions.prompt: Within physiological limits, what happens to stroke volume when preload increases while afterload and inotropic state remain constant?
options: It increases through the Frank-Starling response
It decreases because the ventricle contains more blood
It stays fixed because inotropic state is unchanged
It becomes equal to the entire end-diastolic volume
questions.explanation: Under the stated controls, additional initial stretch supports greater ejection through the Frank-Starling response. An unchanged inotropic state does not make stroke volume insensitive to filling. Keep the prediction within the physiological range given in the stem; it is not a claim that unlimited filling helps or that the ventricle empties completely.
misconceptions: Reverses the controlled relationship between physiological filling and stroke volume.
Assumes only changes in intrinsic contractility can alter stroke volume.
Assumes greater preload eliminates all end-systolic residual volume.

concepts.title: Afterload and the ejection load
concepts.objective: Distinguish afterload from preload and predict the isolated effect of increased ejection load.
concepts.lesson: Afterload describes the mechanical load opposing ventricular ejection. For introductory left ventricular problems, aortic pressure is an important contributor: the ventricle must exceed that pressure to open the aortic valve. Afterload is more fully described by myocardial wall stress, so pressure is a useful cue rather than a complete definition. In a controlled comparison with the same preload and inotropic state, higher afterload tends to reduce stroke volume and leave more blood at end-systole. Separate the timing from preload: preload concerns the starting stretch, while afterload concerns the load during ejection. Real circulation includes interacting responses, so use the controls stated in a question.
key_points: Afterload is the mechanical load opposing ejection, not the initial filling volume.
Aortic pressure is an important contributor to left ventricular afterload.
At fixed preload and inotropy, increased afterload tends to reduce stroke volume and increase residual end-systolic volume.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e: Cardiac Physiology
Richard E. Klabunde: Effects of Preload, Afterload and Inotropy

questions.prompt: A controlled left ventricular model starts each beat at the same filling volume and inotropic state. Raising aortic pressure primarily increases which determinant?
questions.explanation: Higher aortic pressure raises the pressure the left ventricle must overcome to eject, increasing its afterload in this model. Initial filling volume and inotropic state are controlled, so they cannot explain the intervention. Distinguish the resistance encountered during ejection from the filling state at the start of the beat.
misconceptions: Confuses increased outlet pressure with increased initial filling.
Interprets increased mechanical load as increased inotropic state.
Confuses arterial outlet pressure with blood returning to the heart.

questions.prompt: In an isolated model, afterload increases while preload and inotropic state stay constant. Which combination is expected?
options: Higher stroke volume and lower end-systolic volume
Lower stroke volume and higher end-systolic volume
Higher stroke volume and higher end-systolic volume
Unchanged stroke volume and unchanged end-systolic volume
questions.explanation: A greater opposing load makes ejection more difficult at the same initial filling and inotropic state. Less blood is expelled, so stroke volume falls and residual end-systolic volume rises. At a fixed end-diastolic volume, these changes are linked by subtraction: more remaining blood means less ejected blood.
misconceptions: Reverses the effect of an increased ejection load.
Makes ejected and residual volumes rise together despite fixed initial volume.
Assumes afterload cannot alter ejection when inotropic state is unchanged.

questions.prompt: In a simplified normal-valve model, left ventricular pressure is 95 mmHg, left atrial pressure is 10 mmHg, and aortic pressure is 105 mmHg. What prevents aortic ejection at that instant?
options: The ventricular pressure is already above aortic pressure
The mitral valve must open before aortic ejection
The ventricular pressure has not exceeded aortic pressure
The atrial pressure must exceed aortic pressure first
questions.explanation: The aortic valve requires a forward pressure gradient from ventricle to aorta. Here, 95 mmHg is below 105 mmHg, so that opening condition has not been met. Being above atrial pressure explains closure of the mitral inlet, but it does not establish that the ventricular outlet can open.
misconceptions: Reverses the numerical comparison between ventricular and aortic pressures.
Treats opening the ventricular inlet as a requirement for ventricular ejection.
Uses atrial rather than ventricular pressure to determine the aortic valve gradient.

concepts.title: Contractility and inotropic state
concepts.objective: Identify a change in inotropic state at matched loading conditions and calculate its effect on stroke volume.
concepts.lesson: Contractility, or inotropic state, concerns the muscle's ability to develop force under comparable loading conditions. To distinguish it from a filling effect, compare beats with the same preload and afterload. Greater inotropy generally permits more blood to be ejected, reducing end-systolic volume and increasing stroke volume. A stronger beat after additional filling can instead reflect the Frank-Starling response; increased force alone does not prove that inotropy changed. Treat a controlled experiment as a comparison with two of the three determinants held steady. Identify the changed determinant, then connect the residual volume to the ejected volume. These controlled comparisons explain mechanisms before adding the interactions of real circulation.
key_points: Compare contractility at matched loading conditions.
At fixed preload and afterload, greater inotropy generally lowers end-systolic volume and raises stroke volume.
A filling-related increase in force is insufficient evidence of altered inotropic state.

sources.title: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology 2e: Cardiac Physiology
Richard E. Klabunde: Effects of Preload, Afterload and Inotropy

questions.prompt: Which controlled observation best supports increased ventricular inotropic state?
options: More blood ejected at the same preload and afterload
More blood ejected after preload rises, with inotropic state fixed
Less blood ejected after aortic pressure rises
A faster heart rate with no measurement of ventricular ejection
questions.explanation: Matching preload and afterload removes the two loading explanations from this comparison. Greater ejection under those conditions supports increased inotropic state. More ejection after increased filling can reflect Frank-Starling behavior, while altered outlet pressure changes afterload. Heart rate alone does not describe the ventricular muscle's ejection performance.
misconceptions: Uses a controlled filling response as evidence of altered inotropy.
Confuses an increased opposing load with greater intrinsic force-generating ability.
Uses rate alone as evidence of increased ventricular contractility.

questions.prompt: At the same end-diastolic volume of 130 mL and the same afterload, increased inotropy lowers end-systolic volume from 60 to 45 mL. How does stroke volume change?
questions.explanation: Initially, stroke volume is 130 − 60 = 70 mL/beat. After the change it is 130 − 45 = 85 mL/beat. More effective ejection leaves less residual blood. Because initial filling is unchanged, the lower end-systolic volume produces an equal increase in the amount ejected during the beat.
misconceptions: Reverses the relationship between residual volume and ejected volume.
Assumes unchanged initial filling fixes stroke volume despite changed residual volume.
Treats the full initial volume as the ejected volume and adds the residual-volume change.

questions.prompt: Experiment A increases filling while holding inotropic state fixed. Experiment B increases inotropic state while holding filling fixed. Both increase stroke volume at fixed afterload. Which interpretation fits?
options: Both experiments prove that preload increased
A shows a Frank-Starling response; B shows an inotropic response
A shows an inotropic response; B shows a Frank-Starling response
Both experiments prove that afterload decreased
questions.explanation: The same output change can arise from different mechanisms. Experiment A changes the initial filling state and therefore tests the Frank-Starling response at a stated inotropic state. Experiment B changes inotropy at matched filling. Read the experimental controls before attributing a stronger beat to preload, afterload, or intrinsic contractility.
misconceptions: Attributes both responses to filling even though experiment B holds filling fixed.
Swaps the loading response and the inotropic response.
Infers a load reduction despite afterload being fixed in both experiments.
